title: From the Publisher’s Desk
note: Demo snapshot of public ifanca.org content, for a training session only. Not an official IFANCA dataset. Content may be out of date. Check ifanca.org for current information.

blocks.text: “Seek knowledge even if you have to go as far as China” is a famous saying attributed to Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

Even 1500 years ago, China was recognized for its advancements in education. The first verse revealed to Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) in the Qur’an was “Iqra,” meaning “read.” The subsequent verses emphasize concepts such as seeking ilm (knowledge) and refer to the qalam (pen), a symbol of the preservation and transmission of knowledge through teaching and learning. This highlights the importance Islam places on the pursuit of knowledge as a lifelong endeavor.

Today, understanding halal practices is crucial, especially as modern products have become increasingly complex, often containing hidden ingredients. Unfortunately, education about ethnic and religious dietary laws is rarely taught in schools. While scientific education is secular, religious certifications were not part of university curriculums until recently.

Ten years ago, IFANCA began its mission at Cornell University in collaboration with a professor specializing in kosher education. This initiative eventually led to a partnership with Texas A&M University, resulting in the establishment of The Food Diversity Innovation Program (FDIP). Graduates of this program are equipped with the knowledge of halal requirements for the industry worldwide, enabling them to cater to halal-observant communities and shape the future of food innovation.

Through the IFANCA fellowship program, students engage in research that addresses pressing issues related to food sustainability, nutrition, and cultural culinary traditions. This hands-on approach empowers them to develop innovative solutions that positively impact their communities. Educated individuals can advocate for better policies, lead local initiatives, and inspire others to prioritize health and sustainability, aligning perfectly with the Islamic ethos of knowledge sharing and community service.

As Muslims, it is our duty to uphold the value of education and leverage it as a tool for community empowerment. Initiatives like the IFANCA scholarships not only fund education but also cultivate informed citizens who can address societal challenges and build a more inclusive future, embodying the teachings of our faith.

So, while we no longer need to journey all the way to China to seek knowledge, we can now turn to The Food Diversity Innovation Program (FDIP) within the Department of Food Science and Technology at Texas A&M University, and other ever-growing similar programs closer to home.
